title: Video Game Marketing: Finding Players for an Indie Game
description: A course for game makers who have a game, or a game in progress, and need players to find it. It treats marketing as matching a game to the people who will love it: choosing a hook and a genre, studying the market on Steam, building a store page, earning wishlists, and using festivals, trailers, press, streamers and community before and after launch. Claims about how Steam works come from Valve's own Steamworks documentation, and rules of thumb from consultants and developers are labeled as such, with ranges. You market one small indie game through the whole book and finish with a written launch plan.
prerequisites: A game you are making or have made, or the pocket card game from Game Design: Systems, Mechanics, and Player Experience (GDS 201)
Familiarity with Steam as a player
objectives: Write a one-sentence hook and a positioning statement that place a game against three comparable titles.
Estimate a genre's market on Steam from comparable games' release dates, prices and review counts, and state the limits of the estimate.
Plan a Steam store page (capsule art brief, short description, screenshots and tags) that meets current Steamworks rules.
Explain how wishlists, Steam's discovery features and events affect visibility, citing Steamworks documentation.
Plan a demo and a Steam Next Fest entry, and script a trailer that shows the hook in its opening seconds.
Build a press kit and a targeted list of outlets and creators, with a short pitch.
Write a launch and post-launch plan covering release date, price, discounts, updates and community.

preface:
This book is for people who make games and want players to find them. Maybe you have a game half built, or a finished one that launched to silence. Making the game is the hard part, but on a store that adds new games every day, a good game can still go unseen. Marketing, done honestly, is the work of making sure the players who would love your game get the chance to see it.

We focus on Steam, because that is where most small PC games find their players, and we take Valve at its word where it has documented how its store works. Where the advice comes from developers and consultants instead (how many wishlists you need, how many sales a review means), I will say so and give you a range, not a magic number. An academic marketing textbook keeps us grounded in the concepts, and real launches, good and bad, keep us honest.

Our running example is the pocket card game from the Game Design book, now made into a small digital game: a solo card game about keeping a lighthouse lit through a storm. Each chapter adds one part to its marketing plan, from the hook in Chapter 1 to the launch plan in Chapter 8. If you have your own game, use it instead; every exercise works either way.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a marketer who has helped ship small games: platform facts come from Valve's Steamworks documentation, marketing concepts from the academic textbook by Zackariasson and Dymek, and rules of thumb from practitioners such as Chris Zukowski, labeled as practitioner advice and given with their uncertainty.
bible.promise: By the last page you will have a hook, a store page plan, a wishlist and festival strategy, a trailer script, a press and creator list and a launch plan for your own game, and you will know which parts rest on Valve's documentation and which on industry rules of thumb.
threads: Marketing starts with the game: a clear hook in a genre players already want does more than any campaign.
Know the source: Valve's documentation, practitioner data, or guesswork; every number comes with a date and a range.
Steam is the main stage for small PC games, and its rules change, so check the current Steamworks page.
Avoid survivorship bias: study the games that struggled, not only the hits.
One plan, built a chapter at a time, for one running example.

runningExamples.name: The lighthouse card game
runningExamples.use: The pocket card game from Game Design: Systems, Mechanics, and Player Experience (GDS 201), made into a small single-player PC game about keeping a lighthouse lit through a storm, built by a team of one or two. A worked example, not a real product; readers with their own game substitute it in every exercise.

runningExamples.name: The marketing plan
runningExamples.use: One document the reader builds a section per chapter (hook, market summary, store page, visibility plan, festival calendar, trailer script, press list, launch plan). Its store text is also a good project for Creativity and Inspiration (WRT 101).

runningExamples.name: Real Steam games as case studies
runningExamples.use: Published games whose results are public through the developers' own postmortems, talks or Valve's documentation; numbers are cited to their source, never invented.

conventions: Italicize game titles and give the release year at first mention, as in the Game Design book.
Cite Steamworks documentation by page name with the month and year it was checked; asset sizes, discount rules and event rules change.
Give practitioner numbers (wishlist conversion, review multipliers, list thresholds) as ranges from a named source and year, never as laws.
Use Steam's own terms: wishlist, Coming Soon page, capsule, tags, discovery queue, Steam Next Fest.
Money in US dollars with the year.
Refer to Game Design (GDS 201) by chapter title when using its ideas (core loops, playtesting).

bible.care: Steam's rules, sizes and features change; every platform claim cites the current Steamworks page and the date it was checked. Practitioner numbers (wishlist conversion, review multipliers, Popular Upcoming thresholds) vary widely by genre and year, so give ranges and sources, never guarantees, and say plainly that most games sell modestly. Teach honest marketing only: no fake or incentivized reviews, review manipulation, or bought wishlists, followers or traffic, all of which break Steam's rules; capsule art and trailers show the real game. Paid deals with creators must be disclosed (in the US under the FTC's endorsement guides; other countries have similar rules). Present failures alongside hits to avoid survivorship bias.
